newsitem.title: FRANCE: "Carlos" defiant in rare Paris court appearance.
newsitem.headline: "Carlos" defiant in rare Paris court appearance.

text.p: Guerrilla mastermind "Carlos the Jackal, undaunted after more than two years of detention in France, hit out at his captors on Monday and fenced verbally with the judge in a rare courtroom appearance.

Dressed in an open-neck white shirt and a navy jacket, the heavily built, moustachioed Carlos, 47, casually leaned forward, resting his elbows on the edge of the dock as he protested what he called a French travesty of justice.
Judge Martine Anzani turned down his bid to be released in a an investigation into two railway bombings in 1983.

The Venezuelan-born "professional revolutionary", held since he was seized by French counter-espionage in Sudan in August 1994, said investigators had nothing to link him to the bombing of a railway station in the Mediterranean port of Marseille in 1983 and the bombing of a high speed train the same day. Four people died in the two attacks.

The investigation of the two incidents is among several probes reopened by France after Carlos's arrest. Others included an explosion on a Paris-Toulouse train in 1982 in which five people died. His boldest attack was the kidnapping of 11 OPEC oil ministers in Vienna in 1975.
Carlos began on Monday by apologising to Judge Anzani for his heavily accented French.

"Forgive my French but I have been held in France for 2-1/2 years and I am prevented from studying. But with radio and television I have tried to improve," Carlos, who is accused by France of killing 83 people in Europe and the Middle East, said.

Anzani had earlier detailed a probe including intelligence reports from Hungary and then-East Germany where Carlos is believed to have been based, and letters alleged to have been written by him and referring to a series of attacks in France.

Carlos denied writing a letter received by a news agency after the two bombings which referred to a French air force raid on the Lebanon. But he branded the raid "a war crime committed by a president of the French state, Francois Mitterrand".

The four paramilitary gendarmers flanking him stood stone-faced as he denounced police officers as "rotten and ready to sell their mother". He alsop rejected an expert opinion on letters attributed to him because it was based on photocopies.
"People are trying to justify my being placed under investigation and my preventive custody on things like that -- it's rubbish," Carlos said, glancing occasionally at notes.

A comment that Judge Jean-Louis Bruguiere, France's chief anti-terrorism investigator, "likes showing off" earned him a sharp rebuke from Anzani: "It's not because there are people here that you are going to put on a show."

Carlos, his complexion slightly flushed as he brushed away repeated attempts by the judge to cut him short, dismissed the French investigations as "a travesty. I refuse to cooperate, I'm not an informer".

The judge quoted him as telling investigators during questioning about the bombings: "I am not going to give details of conversations at the Elysee (presidential palace) between president Francois Mitterrand and Arab heads of state".

Earlier, Carlos sat stroking his moustache and biting his lower lip as his lawyer Frederic Pariente demanded: "These probes are maintained by pure artifice...Why are the other organisations behind these events not questioned?"
"The authorities judged that it was right to seize (Carlos) and on the other hand an accord is signed with these organisations which provides for a truce," Pariente said.
